sections.text: Parasola plicatilis (Curtis) Redhead, Vilgalys & Hopple (Polish: parasolka fałdowana, czernidłak fałdowany) is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Initially cylindrical, 5–10 mm in diameter, then successively ellipsoid or egg-shaped, hemispherically convex, horizontally flattened, and flat-convex with a slightly depressed centre. When mature it reaches a diameter of up to 3.5 cm. At first smooth, later deeply grooved from the margin almost to the centre. The gills show through, appearing in mature specimens as deep, radiating, parallel furrows. The surface is at first yellowish-honey to pale brown, later grey, with only the centre tinged cinnamon. The margin quickly becomes crenate. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, cylindrical, delicate and hollow inside. The base is slightly thickened and somewhat woolly. The surface is smooth, sometimes slightly longitudinally silky. The colour is whitish at first, then pale ochre. No ring. Gills: Fairly distant, notched, thin, up to 2 mm wide, sometimes slightly bulging. In young fruiting bodies the edges are fringed. At first white, then grey from the spores, finally deliquescing. Flesh: Very thin and brittle, white. No distinct smell or taste. Microscopic features: Spore print black.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: A widespread species. It occurs on all continents except South America and Antarctica. Władysław Wojewoda, in his 2003 list of the large fungi of Poland, does not give its localities, because this species is common throughout Poland. Saprotroph. It occurs in deciduous forests, parks, gardens, at forest edges and by roadsides. Fruiting bodies grow on the ground among grasses, from April to October. It prefers substrates rich in organic matter, especially nitrogen compounds. They usually appear after prolonged rain.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter up to 13 cm. In young specimens gently arched with a distinctly inrolled margin, later flat or somewhat concave, but still with an inrolled margin. The colour is yellow-brown, olive, ochre-brown or red-brown. Young specimens have a slightly felty cap, which later becomes bald. When damaged, the cap skin is spotted dark brown. In dry weather the cap is dry and shiny, in wet weather it becomes very slimy. Gills: Thin, crowded and clearly decurrent on the stem. Wavy in young mushrooms. They are yellowish or rusty and turn brown when damaged. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 1–2 cm. Cylindrical, thick, solid, bare and sometimes narrowed in the lower part. The colour is similar to that of the cap, usually slightly paler. It turns brown when damaged. Flesh: Yellow, yellowish-white or pale ochre, at first firm, later soft; after the mushroom is cut it changes colour to red-brown or rusty brown. The taste is slightly sour, the smell not very intense. Spore print: Ochre-brown. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 8–18 × 4.5–6 µm. Similar species: Similar to Paxillus filamentosus (Polish: krowiak olszowy).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere in areas with a temperate climate. In Europe it is common. It appears in autumn and summer in all types of forest. It grows under various tree species, e.g. birch, oak, alder, pine and spruce. It usually occurs in groups.
Peniophora quercina (Pers.) Cooke (Polish: powłocznica dębowa) is a species of fungus in the family Peniophoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting bodies: Annual, spread out or spread out with a reflexed edge. Single ones are circular in shape, but neighbouring fruiting bodies often merge to form a uniform crust. They are firmly attached to the substrate. In drought they shrink and crack. The thickness of the fruiting bodies is 0.2–2 mm and varies with the weather; they are thicker in wet weather and thinner in dry weather. In young specimens the whole surface of the fruiting body adheres to the substrate and its margin is delicately fringed, whitish and fibrous; in older fruiting bodies the margin lifts away from the substrate and curls back. The outer side of the fruiting body that lifts away from the substrate is rough, uneven and dark brown or black, on oaks growing in wet terrain violet-blue. Hymenophore: Covers the whole surface of the fruiting body. It is smooth, wrinkled, knobbly, matt, radially folded, and cracked in older fruiting bodies. The colour is grey-pink, light brown or grey-violet, turning brown in older specimens. Flesh: Very thin. Soft and waxy in young specimens, brittle and leathery in older ones. Spore print: Pink. Spores cylindrical, with a pointed base and bent into a sausage shape.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It is common in Europe and has also been recorded in Asia. It grows mainly on the bark of oaks (especially pedunculate oak), rarely on grey alder, lime and beech. It occurs in deciduous and mixed forests and in parks. It colonises mainly dead, fallen branches and dead trunks and stumps. It is common throughout Poland (except in the mountains, where it is rare).
Phaeolus schweinitzii (Fr.) Pat. (Polish: murszak rdzawy) is a species of fungus in the family Laetiporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: An annual bracket fungus consisting of a cap and a stem. It produces single fruiting bodies or groups in which the fruiting bodies often fuse at their bases. Cap: Circular, semicircular, kidney-shaped or irregular in shape, 8–30 cm wide, 1–4 cm thick. The margin is wavy or inrolled, cut in places and usually without hymenophore. The surface is uneven, wrinkled and knobbly, at first felty, hairy or shaggy, becoming bare with age. The margin is sulphur-yellow or yellow-ochre, the centre from orange to dark red, the base almost black. Stem: Short, lateral or central, funnel-shaped or flattened. It is covered with hymenophore. Dimensions: 3–8 × 2–5 cm. Flesh: 1–1.5 cm thick. In young fruiting bodies spongy and juicy, hardening with time. After drying it becomes fibrous and corky, brittle and light. The colour is orange to brown; it darkens when pressed or under the influence of KOH. It has a weak smell and a sourish taste. Hymenophore: Tubular, maze-like, yellow, rusty yellow, ochre or olive-green. The tubes are up to 1 cm long and form only one layer, which also runs down the stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is distributed mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, but also occurs in Australia, and has also been recorded in western Central Africa. It grows on the roots, trunks and stumps of various coniferous trees, usually at the base of still living trunks. In Poland it is common.
Phallus hadriani Vent. (Polish: sromotnik fiołkowy) is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Young fruiting bodies: in the form of a spherical or egg-shaped egg. The mature fruiting body (receptacle) consists of a volva and a stem up to 20 cm long, usually 6–10 cm. The colour of the covering is violetish or pinkish. It has a weaker smell than Phallus impudicus. Flesh: The flesh of the stem is whitish, spongy, with numerous chambers, very brittle. Similar species: Phallus impudicus is very similar. It differs in its less violet colouring, smaller disc at the top of the cap, stronger smell and place of occurrence.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It grows on sandy, dry coastal dunes on the Baltic coast, sporadically inland. Fruiting bodies appear in summer and autumn. Very rare.
Phallus impudicus L. (Polish: sromotnik smrodliwy) is a species of fungus in the family Phallaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Young fruiting body: This is a fungus of unusual structure. The fruiting body of young specimens is spherical or egg-shaped, white or cream, sometimes with a yellow tinge. It measures 4–6 × 3–5 cm and is attached to the substrate by mycelium resembling fairly thick cords. It is partly hidden underground. This is the so-called egg, also commonly called the devil's egg. In cross-section the beginning of the fruiting body can already be seen inside the egg's covering. During development the egg bursts and the more typical mature fruiting body (the so-called receptacle) appears. Young fruiting bodies have a faint smell similar to that of radish. In appearance they resemble puffballs, but differ from them in the covering; it consists of two layers, between which there is a gelatinous mass. As the fungus matures the mass becomes more liquid and, after the covering tears, covers the head of the receptacle. Receptacle: It is 10–30 cm tall, cylindrical, narrow at the top, porous, fragile and hollow inside. It is white, with a volva at the base and a poorly differentiated head at the top. The head resembles morels in appearance. It is a dozen or so cm long, cone- or thimble-shaped, and covered with a green gelatinous mass in which the spores are found.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere in the temperate climate zone, and also in South America and Asia (Japan, Ceylon, Java). In Poland it is common. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows singly or in groups in parks, forests and thickets and is fairly common everywhere (except at higher mountain elevations).
Phellinus igniarius (L.) Quél (Polish: czyreń ogniowy) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: It attaches to the substrate by its side; no stem. Width 15–25 cm, thickness 8–15 cm, the shape at first bulbous, later flat or hoof-shaped. The surface is grey, darkening with time, sometimes cracked. It is smooth or finely suede-like, sometimes green from algae growing on it, and irregularly, concentrically zoned. The skin is hard, the cap margin broad and rounded. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes form many layers, each up to 5 mm thick. They are the same colour as the fruiting body, or paler. The pores of the tubes are very small, round. Flesh: Up to 2 cm thick. It is woody, zoned and dark rusty brown to chestnut brown. Spore print: White. Spores colourless, measuring 4–6.5 × 4–5.5 μm. Similar species: Fomes fomentarius (Polish: hubiak pospolity). It has softer and paler flesh and is not as firmly attached to the trunk. Phellinus hartigii (Polish: czyreń jodłowy), but it grows mainly on firs; Phellinus tremulae (Polish: czyreń osikowy), but it grows only on aspen

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe, Asia and the Canary Islands. In Poland it is very common, both in the lowlands and at lower mountain elevations. A tree-dwelling fungus. It occurs most often in riverside forests, along streams, but also in orchards, gardens and various types of forests and thickets. It grows mainly on willows, but also on other deciduous trees; on beech, hornbeam and others. It also attacks fruit trees.
Phellinus pomaceus (Pers.) Maire (Polish: czyreń śliwowy) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial, of very varied shape. It may be spread out (resupinate), spread out and reflexed, cushion-shaped, knobbly, hoof-shaped, hemispherical, and also irregular in shape. The size is usually up to a few cm; often individual fruiting bodies fuse together or occur one above another like roof tiles, forming large clusters. The surface of young fruiting bodies is sandy-ochre, later through cinnamon-yellow and yellowish-brown it becomes chestnut, finally grey and almost black. It is at first slightly mossy, but quickly becomes smooth, later cracked. The margin of the fruiting body (the growth zone) is blunt, paler and lacks hymenophore. Hymenophore: Tubular, multilayered. Tubes 2–3 mm long, rusty brown, in older fruiting bodies sometimes overgrown with mycelium. Pores yellow-ochre, later rusty, finally brown. They are round or angular, sometimes elongated, 1–2 mm in diameter. Flesh: Yellow-brown or rusty brown, corky or woody. Spore print: White. Spores almost spherical, with slightly pointed ends, a smooth surface and measuring 5–7 × 4–5.5 µm. Setae very few, hard to notice.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe and some regions of South America, Africa and Asia. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling fungus. It grows mainly on fruit trees, especially in neglected orchards, most often on plums, but sometimes also on apricots, cherries, apple trees and pear trees. It grows on trunks and branches (mainly on their lower side).
Phellodon tomentosus (L.) Banker (Polish: korkoząb kieliszkowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Thelephoraceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: A single one is circular with a depressed centre and 2–6 cm in diameter, but neighbouring caps often fuse into an irregular cap reaching a diameter of up to 20 cm. The surface is matt, felty, with fibres growing over it radially. It is concentrically zoned, darker in the middle, grey or reddish-brown, the margin whitish. Hymenophore: Spiny. The spines are up to 3 mm long and run slightly down the stem. They are white in young fruiting bodies, greyish in older ones. Stem: Height 1–3 cm, thickness up to 0.8 cm. Cylindrical, straight or twisted. The surface is light brown to dark brown. Neighbouring stems are often joined by compact mycelium that also grows through the substrate. Flesh: Light brown in the cap, reddish or dark brown in the stem. It is zoned. The taste and smell are bitterish; when drying it smells like the spice maggi. Spores: Whitish, spherical and slightly angular, with a surface covered in spines. Dimensions: 3–5 × 2.5–4 μm. Similar species: Phellodon niger (Polish: korkoząb czarniawy). It has darker fruiting bodies, from blue-black to grey-black; Phellodon confluens (Polish: korkoząb pozrastany).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents of the Northern Hemisphere and on some islands; it has not been recorded in the Southern Hemisphere. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is E – endangered species. It is also on lists of threatened species in Germany, Denmark, England and the Netherlands. It grows on the ground, in coniferous and mixed forests, also in urban forests, on needle litter and among bilberry undershrubs. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November. Saprotroph.
Phlebia radiata Fr. (Polish: żylak promienisty) is a species of fungus in the family Meruliaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: A tremelloid fungus. Fruiting bodies up to 8 mm thick, at first circular or oval, later spreading widely. They are spread out flat and entirely attached to the substrate, less often with a reflexed margin. The margin is ragged. As they grow, individual fruiting bodies fuse with neighbouring ones, covering a considerable area. The colour is pale flesh-pink or orange-reddish, with distinct veins or folds of the hymenophore radiating outwards. Hymenophore: In the form of radiating folds and veins. Pale pink, orange to red, darkening with age to brown or turning grey. Flesh: Gelatinous or fleshy-waxy. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical, granular and smooth, measuring 4.5–6 × 1.5–2.5 μm. Similar species: Phlebia tremellosa (Polish: żylak trzęsakowaty) has a similar underside of the fruiting body, but unlike Phlebia radiata, which adheres closely to the substrate, it usually forms small caps or projecting lobes. The żylica olbrzymia is also similar.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Most localities of Phlebia radiata have been described in North America and Europe, but it also occurs in South America, Africa and New Zealand. In Poland it is fairly common. A tree-dwelling fungus, saprotroph. It occurs in forests, parks, gardens and orchards. It grows on stumps and on trunks and branches lying on the ground, mainly on the wood of deciduous trees: Alnus glutinosa, Betula pendula, Carpinus, Fagus, Populus tremula, Quercus petraea, Duercus sp., Salix caprea, Sorbus aucuparia, Tilia, less often on coniferous trees: on silver fir, Norway spruce and cultivated black pine.
Pholiota aurivella (Batsch) P. Kumm. (Polish: łuskwiak złotawy) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–12 cm. In young individuals conical, later hemispherical, and finally flat. It is golden-yellow or rusty yellow with darker, adpressed patches. On young mushrooms there are remains of the partial veil at the cap margin, but they are fairly quickly washed away by rain. In wet weather and in young specimens the cap surface is sticky and even slimy. Gills: White when young, then olive and rusty brown with a serrated edge, adnexed to the stem or slightly notched with a tooth. Stem: Height 10–12 cm, thickness up to 1 cm. It is fibrous and the same colour as the cap, or slightly paler. Its ring consists of brown threads forming a woolly annulus, which later partly disappears. Below the ring it is covered with brown fibrils, above it is yellowish and downy. Flesh: Yellowish in the cap, slightly darker in the stem, odourless and not changing colour when damaged. It has a mild taste. Spore print: Rusty brown. Spores measuring 8 × 5–6 μm, ellipsoid, smooth. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe, Korea, Japan, Morocco and New Zealand. In Poland it is common throughout the country, both in the lowlands and in the mountains. A tree-dwelling fungus, saprotroph and parasite. It grows on dead and living deciduous trees; it has been found on the following tree species and genera: sycamore maple, horse chestnut, alder, silver birch, hornbeam, beech, walnut, poplar, acacia, white willow, elm, and only exceptionally on fir. It produces fruiting bodies from April to October.
Pholiota flammans (Batsch) P. Kumm (Polish: łuskwiak ognisty) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–6 cm. In young individuals hemispherical, then hemispherically arched, finally flat-arched. It long retains an inrolled margin. The surface is dry, slightly slimy in wet weather, lemon-yellow to orange. It is entirely covered with large, uniformly coloured scales, which also hang from the cap margin. Gills: Crowded, lemon-yellow in young fruiting bodies, then darkening to olive, finally rusty brown. Stem: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 0.8 cm. Cylindrical, solid in young fruiting bodies, hollow in older ones. It is smooth only in a narrow zone under the cap; elsewhere it is entirely covered with spreading sulphur-coloured fibres. Flesh: Sulphur-yellow, rusting slightly only near the margins. The taste is bitterish, the smell somewhat radish-like. Microscopic features: Spore print brown. Spores yellowish, elliptical, smooth, without a germ pore, amyloid. Pleurocystidia of various shapes, up to 40 μm long; some are filled inside with uniform dark brown content, others stain under KOH like chrysocystidia. The numerous cheilocystidia, also of various shapes, are up to 20 μm long.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A species widespread in North America and Europe. It also occurs in Asia, where its occurrence is less well studied. In Asia it has been recorded in Japan, India and China. It grows in various types of forests and parks, on trunks and stumps of coniferous trees, especially pine and spruce. Fruiting bodies, produced from August to October, grow singly or in small groups.
Pholiota squarrosa (Vahl) P. Kumm. (Polish: łuskwiak nastroszony) is a species of fungus in the family pierścieniakowate.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–15 cm. In young individuals egg-shaped and closed, later hemispherical, and finally flat. It is ochre, ochre-brown to brown, darker in the middle. The surface is densely covered with spreading scales. The margin is inrolled for a long time. Gills: Yellowish when young, then rusty brown. They are crowded, slightly decurrent and attached to the stem. Stem: Height 4–8 cm, thickness up to 12 mm. Fibrous and the same colour as the cap. It has a ring. Below the ring it is covered with scales, like the cap. Flesh: Yellowish, not changing colour when damaged. It has a mild taste somewhat resembling that of radish. Spore print: Brown. Spores measuring 6–8 × 3.5–4 μm. Smooth, ellipsoid. Similar species: Most similar is Pholiota squarrosoides (Polish: łuskwiak rdzawołuskowy). It has a pale cap margin and grows only on dead beech wood. Somewhat similar is Gymnopilus junionus (Polish: łysak wspaniały). It has very bitter flesh, and its cap and stem have no scales. Less experienced mushroom pickers may confuse it with Armillaria mellea. It has only small scales, which are easily rubbed off with a finger, and its fruiting bodies are also less massive.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe and Asia. In Poland it is common. It grows on fallen wood or at the base of living trees, both deciduous and coniferous, though on coniferous ones much more rarely. It occurs in clumps, from summer to autumn. It is associated with the trees: silver birch, hornbeam, beech, European ash, white poplar, Hungarian oak, Quercus sp., black locust, willow, Japanese pagoda tree, rowan, small-leaved lime, Tilia sp., rarely silver fir. It produces fruiting bodies from June to November.
Phyllotopsis nidulans (Pers.) Singer (Polish: boczniaczek pomarańczowożółty) is a species of fungus in the order Agaricales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Length 3–7 cm, width 2–5 cm, kidney-shaped, shell-shaped, usually attached by its side, sometimes spread out. No stem; sometimes in its place there is only an elongated part of the cap covered with white bristles. The surface is felty or velvety, the margin inrolled, downy. When dry it is light ochre-yellow, when wet orange-yellow. Gills: Radiating and eccentric, broad, decurrent. They are orange to rusty yellow with smooth edges. Flesh: Thin, springy, yellow. The smell is mild, the taste indistinct or slightly mushroomy. Spore print: Very pale pink to pink-brown. Spores elliptical, elongated, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 5–8 × 2–4 μm. Similar species: Tapinella panuoides (Polish: ponurnik bocznotrzonowy) lacks such an intense orange colour; Sarcomyxa serotina (Polish: śluzołycznik późny) has a small stem, is olive-green and occurs only on deciduous trees, and its fruiting bodies are also larger.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – species vulnerable to extinction. It is also on lists of threatened species in Austria, Belgium, Germany and Denmark. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests on old, rotting trees and on dead trunks and stumps, both deciduous and coniferous. It has been recorded on hornbeams, beeches, walnut, rowans, limes, wych elm, firs, spruces and pines. It produces fruiting bodies from April to October.
Picipes badius (Pers.) Zmitr. & Kovalenko (Polish: czarnostopka kasztanowa) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Initially inrolled, later spread out, finally funnel-shaped. The shape is circular, shell-shaped or kidney-shaped. It reaches a width of 5–10 cm, but sometimes even 20 cm. It is thin – 1–3 mm thick – with a sharp and usually wavy margin. Sometimes 2 or more caps grow from one stem. The skin is gelatinous, since it is made of hyphae stuck together, smooth and bare, shiny in dry weather. The upper surface of young fruiting bodies is olive or olive-brown, in older ones it becomes purple-brown, chestnut, black-brown, even black, especially in the middle of the cap. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes run slightly down the stem. They are 0.5–2.5 mm long and form one layer. In young fruiting bodies they are white, in older ones they change colour to cream or nut-coloured. The pores are round and very small, with 4–7 per mm. Stem: Short and fairly thin (relative to the size of the cap). It is 2–2.3 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick. It is usually eccentric, less often lateral or central. It is entirely black and suede-like, covered with an easily detached down. Flesh: Fleshy-leathery in young fruiting bodies, hardening in older ones.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Africa and Antarctica. In Poland it is moderately common. It develops on wood mainly of deciduous trees, very rarely on coniferous ones. It grows on dead wood, especially on fallen trunks; it prefers willows, poplars, beeches, oaks and hornbeams. Fruiting bodies appear in two flushes: in spring and in autumn. Recently the abundance of this species in Europe has been increasing, which is probably a result of climate warming. A saprotroph causing white rot of wood.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: Polyporus melanopus (Polish: żagiew ciemnonoga), occurring on buried wood of deciduous trees. The cap of a young fruiting body is pale, ochre or grey-brown, shortly hairy; Cerioporus varius (Polish: żagwiak zmienny). It has a black stem only in the lower part, and a cap from yellowish to brown.
Pleurotus dryinus (Pers.) P. Kumm. (Polish: boczniak białożółty) is a species of fungus in the family Pleurotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Convex in young specimens, but quickly spread out. Diameter 6–10 cm, white or pale grey, felty-fibrous or scaly, with membranous remains of the veil on the margin (especially in young fruiting bodies). Gills: Distant, forked near the stem, decurrent on the stem. At first whitish, then yellowing. Stem: Height 1–3 cm, thickness 1 cm, mostly placed eccentrically in relation to the cap. It is whitish and velvety-felty, at first also with membranous remains of the veil. It has a short-lived ring. Flesh: Whitish, yellowing, bast-like. Spore print: White. Spores measuring 9–13 × 3–4 µm in diameter. Similar species: Pleurotus ostreatus (Polish: boczniak ostrygowaty), which has no remains of the veil and no yellowing flesh. Pleurotus calyptratus (Polish: boczniak topolowy), which, however, has a smooth cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe and Asia. In Poland it is fairly frequent; numerous localities throughout the country have been described in the scientific literature. It grows in various types of forests, parks, along roads and on solitary trees, both in villages and in towns. It develops on both dead and living trees (mainly damaged ones). It colonises stumps and trunks of deciduous trees, less often coniferous (in particular fir). It produces annual fruiting bodies from July to October. It is most often found on beeches and oaks.
Pleurotus ostreatus (Jacq.) P. Kumm. (Polish: boczniak ostrygowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Pleurotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5 to 25 cm. The shape is at first arched, with a long inrolled margin, later shell-shaped, fan-shaped or funnel-shaped. It attaches to the substrate by its side. It is soft and springy, the surface smooth and bare, covered with white down only near the stem. The colour is quite varied; it may be in various shades of brown, ash-grey, grey-brown, steel-blue and violet. Gills: Crowded and deeply decurrent on the stem, from whitish to grey, in older specimens even violet. Stem: Short, thick, 1 to 4 cm tall. White or grey in colour. It is bare, covered with bristles only at the base. Flesh: In the cap it is soft in young specimens, springy in older ones; in the stem of older specimens it becomes corky and woody. The colour is white, the taste sourish. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 8–11 × 3–4 µm. Similar species: Pleurotus dryinus (Polish: boczniak białożółty) has a paler, whitish cap with a slightly shaggy surface; Pleurotus cornucopiae (Polish: boczniak rowkowanotrzonowy) has a trumpet-shaped cap and a grooved stem.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling fungus occurring on dead wood of deciduous tree species such as hornbeam, beech, willow, poplar, black locust, birch and walnut. It usually grows in clustered groups. They consist of many larger and smaller specimens, often fused in clumps, resembling shoals of oysters, from which the name of this species comes. Fruiting bodies appear only in late autumn, from the end of October into winter, and when the winter is mild, also in winter.
Pleurotus pulmonarius (Fr.) Quel. (Polish: boczniak łyżkowaty) is a species of fungus in the family Pleurotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–12 cm, spatula-shaped, oyster-shaped in younger specimens, with a bent, sometimes ragged margin, soft, thinly fleshy, pale, cream, pale brown, yellowing at the margin, grey-brown with age, attached by its side to the substrate. The cap margin is inrolled. Gills: Crowded, narrow, springy, deeply decurrent on the stem, unforked, narrow, springy, whitish or pale cream. They turn yellow as they dry. Stem: Height 1–6 cm and thickness 0.6–1.5 cm, eccentric, sometimes lateral. It is conical (thinner at the base). The surface is smooth, whitish, felty at the base. Flesh: With an indistinct smell resembling anise and a sweetish taste, at first springy, delicate, with age tough, whitish. Spore print: White with a violet tinge. Spores cylindrical, 7.5–11 × 3–4 µm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs on all continents except Antarctica and Africa. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – species vulnerable to extinction. A parasitic and saprotrophic fungus. It grows most often on trunks and in the boughs of beeches, also on oaks and other deciduous trees. Fruiting bodies mostly grow in numerous clumps, but single specimens are also found. It produces fruiting bodies from June to October. It occurs on both dead wood and living trees.
Pluteus atromarginatus (Konrad) Kühner (Polish: drobnołuszczak czarnoostrzowy, drobnołuszczak czarnorozwierkowy) is a species of fungus in the family Pluteaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–15 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, then arched, in older ones flat-arched to flat, sometimes also shallowly concave. It has a low, broad umbo or papilla, and a radially fibrillose surface, finely scaly in the middle. The margin sometimes extends beyond the gills. The colour is dark to tobacco-brown, paler at the margin, brownish-grey. Gills: Broad, ventricose, free, at first whitish, then light pink, finally pink-brown to brownish-pink. Edges dark brown. Stem: Height 4–16 cm, thickness 0.6–1.7 cm, cylindrical with the base widened to 2.5 cm, solid. The surface is greyish-white to light brown, covered longitudinally with dark brown fibrils. Flesh: White in the cap, watery, grey-marbled in the stem. The taste is sweetish-mushroomy, the smell unpleasant. Similar species: The characteristic features of this species are its large fruiting body, its occurrence on coniferous trees and the dark edges of the gills. Very similar in colouring is Pluteus pseudorobertianii (Polish: drobnołuszczak czarnołuskowy), but the edges of its gills are not blackish.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, Europe, Asia, Australia and New Zealand. In Poland, W. Wojewoda cited two localities in 2003; in later years numerous new ones have been reported. A saprotroph growing on dead trunks of coniferous trees.
Pluteus aurantiorugosus (Trog) Sacc. (Polish: drobnołuszczak pomarańczowoczerwony, łuskowiec pomarańczowoczerwony) is a species of fungus in the family Pluteaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.5–5 cm, in young specimens, then arched with a blunt umbo, finally spread out, non-hygrophanous. The margin is even, only slightly crenate in older specimens. The surface is smooth or slightly wrinkled, orange. In the middle orange-red, matt when dry. Gills: Free, ventricose, at first white, then light pink. Edges white and fringed. Stem: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 0.6 cm, cylindrical, at first solid, later hollow with a club-shaped widened base. The surface is white to yellowish-white, longitudinally fibrous in young specimens. The base is dark yellow to orange. Flesh: White in the cap, yellowish in the stem, with an indistinct smell and a bitter taste. Microscopic features: Spore print pink. Spores 5.5–8 × 4–5 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline, non-amyloid and not changing colour in KOH. Cheilocystidia sparse, broadly barrel-shaped, thin-walled, measuring up to 50 15 µm. Pileocystidia with swollen terminal elements. Clamp connections absent.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Asia. W. Wojewoda, in his 2003 list of the large fungi of Poland, cites only two localities of it. More and more recent localities are given by the online mushroom atlas. In Poland this species is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is E – a species threatened with extinction, whose survival is unlikely if the threatening factors continue to operate. A saprotrophic fungus. It occurs in deciduous forests on rotting wood of deciduous trees, especially maples, ashes, elms and poplars.
Pluteus cervinus (Schaeff.) P. Kumm. (Polish: drobnołuszczak jeleni, drobnołuszczak porysowany, łuskowiec jeleni) is a species of fungus in the family Pluteaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–12 cm, sometimes even up to 15 cm; at first hemispherical, later convex, finally flat. Sometimes it has a blunt umbo, sometimes the centre of the cap is wrinkled or knobbly. The surface is silky or with fine, embedded fibrils. The colour of the cap is in various shades of brown and grey, from light grey-brown to black-brown; albino individuals with a completely white cap also occur. In wet weather it is shiny. Gills: Free (not reaching the stem). Cream-white in young specimens, then salmon-pink, fairly crowded, ventricose. Stem: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm, but specimens with a stem up to 3 cm thick sometimes occur. Cylindrical, less often club-shaped. The surface is dirty white with darker fibrils forming longitudinal streaks. Solid in youth, hollow in old specimens. Flesh: Whitish, elastic in the cap, fairly brittle in the stem. The taste is mild, somewhat musty or earthy, the smell fairly strong, similar to radish or potato sprouts. Microscopic features: Spore print pink. Spores broadly ellipsoid, smooth, measuring (6.5) 7.5 × 6.5 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Africa and Antarctica it occurs on all continents, and also on many islands. In North America and Central Europe it is frequent. In Poland it is very common. It occurs in forests, coniferous as well as deciduous and mixed. It grows on rotting wood; on trunks, thicker branches lying on the ground, on bark, on sawdust and on various kinds of wood chips, but never on thin branches. Fruiting bodies appear from spring to late autumn, singly or in small groups (a few specimens).
Pluteus salicinus (Pers.) P. Kumm. (Polish: drobnołuszczak zielonawowoszary, łuskowiec wierzbowy) is a species of fungus in the family Pluteaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1.3–7 cm, at first convex, later broadly and flatly spread out, usually slightly raised in the middle. The surface is silkily shiny, covered with fine, thread-like fibrils closely bound to the skin. These fibrils are arranged radially, and at the top of the cap their protruding ends form scale-like tufts. The surface is smooth; only in wet weather may the margin be shortly striate. The cap is mouse-grey, sometimes darker at the top, with a greenish tinge. The mouse-grey sometimes shades into olive, or even beige-pink. Completely white specimens occur very rarely. Gills: Crowded, free, fairly broad, bulging. White in young specimens, then with a salmon-pink tinge. The edge is even, slightly cottony-fringed and the same colour. Stem: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 0.3–0.7 cm, with a slightly thickened base. At the base slightly darker streaks are visible, and in the upper part it is silkily shiny. Flesh: Whitish in the cap and the upper part of the stem, ivory-coloured in the lower part of the stem. Smell and taste musty. Microscopic features: Spore print pink with a beige tinge.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread in the United States, the British Isles and Northern Europe. It was first identified in the state of Illinois. In the scientific literature it has been described from numerous localities in various regions of Poland. Saprotroph. It is encountered relatively rarely. It occurs in forests throughout Poland, above all in damp environments such as ravines, oak-hornbeam forests and alder carrs. It appears from July to November on rotting logs and old stumps of deciduous, less often coniferous, wood.
Polyporus tuberaster (Pers.) Fr. (Polish: żagiew guzowata, żagiew Forquignona, żagiew wieńcowa) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 2–12 cm, the shape most often funnel-shaped, sometimes spread out. The skin is dry, felty, light brown, covered with darker (ochre-brown or red-brown) scales. Hymenophore: Tubular. The tubes are white and run down the stem. The pores are large (diameter 1–2 mm), angular, white in young specimens, yellowish in older ones. Stem: Height 3–8 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm, cylindrical, straight or crooked, mostly set in the centre of the cap. The surface is whitish or pale ochre, slightly hairy. Flesh: Elastic in young fruiting bodies, bast-like in older ones, whitish, odourless. Spore print: White. Spores elliptical, smooth, measuring 9.5–14.5 × 3.5–5.8 μm. Similar species: Similar fruiting bodies are produced by Cerioporus squamosus (Polish: żagwiak łuskowaty), but it has no sclerotium. A similar hymenophore is found in the much more common Lentinus brumalis (Polish: żagiew zimowa), which also does not produce a sclerotium.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been confirmed in Europe (in Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Denmark, France, Spain, Ireland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Germany, Norway, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Sweden and Great Britain), in north-western Africa (in Morocco), in North America (in the United States and Canada), and in Australia and Japan. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas.
Polyporus umbellatus (Pers.) Fr. (Polish: żagiew wielogłowa) is a species of fungus in the family Polyporaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: From a common stem grow branched, dense clusters of numerous fruiting bodies, in shape resembling irregular, spherical forms 10–50 cm in diameter. Cap: Diameter 2–4 cm, irregular, with a fibrous-suede and scaly-cracked surface. Scales ochre-brown to grey-brown. Tubes: 1–1.5 mm long, straw-yellow, running far down the stem. Stem: Whitish, sometimes cream, irregularly joined to neighbouring stems, growing from a branched fleshy base – a sclerotium – which takes up nutrients from the substrate. Flesh: Whitish, fleshy; the smell is pleasant, resembling dill; the taste is pleasant, with an astringent aftertaste. Spore print: White. Spores cylindrical, smooth, colourless, 7–10 × 3–4 µm. Similar species: Its individual caps are spatula-shaped, fan-shaped, spatula-shaped, wedge-shaped, without centrally set stems.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: In Poland it is a rare species. By 2020 about 100 of its localities had been reported. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – a vulnerable species which will probably move to the category of endangered species in the near future if the threatening factors continue to operate. It is on lists of threatened species also in Austria, Belgium, Germany, Denmark, Estonia, Lithuania, Norway, the Netherlands, Sweden and Finland. In 1983–2014 it was under strict protection, and since 2014 under partial protection. Harvesting fruiting bodies for commercial purposes is permitted after obtaining the appropriate
Porodaedalea pini (Brot.) Murrill (Polish: czyrogmatwica sosnowa, czyreń sosnowy) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Perennial, of the bracket-fungus type. It grows singly, or several fruiting bodies together, which usually fuse with one another. It attaches to the substrate by its side. At first it is bracket-shaped or semicircular, then hoof-shaped, and in cross-section usually triangular. It reaches a width of up to 20 cm and a height of up to 8 cm. The surface is concentrically zoned, covered with lumps and furrows, quite often radially, deeply cracked. The colour is at first brown or green-brown, later almost black. Sometimes it is overgrown with algae and then the surface is celadon-green. The margin is usually sharp and even, chestnut in young specimens. Over a width of about 0.5–1 mm it is sterile. It has tawny hairs, which fall off in older fruiting bodies. Hymenophore: Tubular, greyish-yellow or yellow-olive in young individuals, rusty in older ones. The tubes are 3–10 mm long and the fruiting body may have several layers of them separated by flesh. They have irregular oval, angular, elongated or somewhat maze-like pores, usually 0.2 to 0.7 mm long, but sometimes up to 3 mm. The pore edges are entire, downy in young specimens. It gives off a strong mushroom smell. Flesh:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is widespread in the Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is fairly frequent. Numerous localities have been reported in the scientific literature. It develops on living trees, mainly on Scots pine, less often on black pine. In Polish literature its occurrence has also been reported on the following cultivated tree species: Lawson's cypress, jack pine, Douglas fir (blue form), western thuja and western hemlock. The fruiting bodies usually grow fairly high on the trunk of trees, mainly older ones. They are most often found in old parks or old stands of trees.
Porphyrellus porphyrosporus (Fr. & Hök) E.-J. Gilbert (Polish: grzybiec purpurowozarodnikowy) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 8–14 cm, hemispherical when young, later convex to almost flat, of round or oval shape. Light grey in youth, darkening early to brown or grey-brown; the surface is matt and finely downy, not slimy. In most cases it is dark and looks smoked. The skin cannot be peeled off and sometimes cracks in old age. Tubes: Young ones pale, greyish-yellow, early grey-brown, staining when damaged; shorter around the stem; the pores are most often small, sometimes also relatively large, and then reach as far as the upper side of the cap. Stem: Height 4–16 cm, thickness 1–4 cm, at first barrel-shaped, later cylindrical. Like the cap it is umber-brown to tar-brown, finely suede-like; relatively slender and thin. Flesh: White or dirty grey-whitish, after cutting it turns slightly greenish-blue (above all above the tubes), and slowly reddens, especially under the skin of the cap. Odourless, with a mild taste. Spore print: Dark reddish-brown. Spores oblong elliptical-spindle-shaped, smooth, measuring 14–20 × 6–8 µm. Similar species: Hard to confuse with other fungus species.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Japan. In Poland it is a rare species. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas. It is on red lists of threatened species also in Belgium, Germany, Estonia, Lithuania, Sweden, Norway and Latvia. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in coniferous and mixed forests, less often in deciduous ones, on the ground, under spruces, firs and beeches, on acid soils, especially in higher-lying regions.
Psathyrella piluliformis (Bull.) P.D. Orton (Polish: kruchaweczka namakająca) is a species of fungus in the family Psathyrellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 2 to 5 cm (exceptionally up to 7 cm). At first bell-shaped, later increasingly spread out, finally flat. The surface is bare, never sticky. On young fruiting bodies there are whitish, delicate remains of the veil, sometimes hanging from the cap margins. It is hygrophanous: when wet it is red-brown or dark brown, when dry ochre-beige. When wet, the cap margins are finely striate (the gills show through). Gills: Crowded, light beige when young, then brown-black (without a violet tinge). Cystidia are situated on the edge and surface of the gills. Stem: Height up to 8 cm, thickness 4–8 mm. Hollow, very fragile, sometimes slightly wavy, uneven. The surface is bare, sometimes with whitish fibrils that are remains of the veil. No ring. In young fruiting bodies the stems are pale, in older ones they darken. Flesh: White and very brittle, with an indistinct smell and taste. Spore print: Black-brown. Spores oval or ellipsoid, measuring 4.5–6.5 × 3–4 µm, without a germ pore. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: A common species in North America and Europe. From Asia its occurrence has been reported in Japan and Taiwan. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling saprotrophic fungus. It grows in forests and parks on deciduous wood, mainly on beeches, hornbeams and oaks. It most often grows on stumps or on trunks and branches lying on the ground. On coniferous wood it is found very rarely. It produces fruiting bodies from August to November, in tufts or in groups.
Pseudoboletus parasiticus (Bull.) Šutara (Polish: borowikowiec tęgoskórowy, podgrzybek tęgoskórowy) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter from 2 to 6 cm. At first semicircular, later cushion-shaped, finally flattened. The surface is coloured from dirty yellow through greenish-ochre to olive-brown, dry, suede-like, sometimes cracked into small patches (especially in dry weather). Tubes: Adnate or slightly decurrent, angular, yellow when young, later brown-olive or brown-yellow. Stem: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 0.4–2 cm. Solid, yellow to yellow-brown or olive, narrowed below and usually strongly curved. It has a fibrillose structure. Flesh: Yellowish, lemon-yellow above the tubes, brownish in the lower part of the stem, turning slightly blue in section. The taste is mild, the smell mushroomy. Spore print: Dark olive. Spores oval-spindle-shaped, pale yellow to honey-yellow, measuring 12–18 × 4.5–6 µm. Similar species: A similar-looking fungus is the so-called Boletus subtomentosus (Polish: podgrzybek zajączek), but the peculiar habitat of Pseudoboletus parasiticus virtually rules out a mistake.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described only in the eastern part of North America and in Europe. In Poland, by 2020 its occurrence had been reported in the mycological literature at about 150 localities. In the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland it is placed in the group of rare species (threat category R). It is on red lists of threatened species also in Belgium, Denmark, Slovakia, Lithuania and Germany. It grows as a parasite on the fruiting bodies of Scleroderma citrinum (Polish: tęgoskór cytrynowy). From one fruiting body of Scleroderma 1–5 fruiting bodies of this bolete grow.
Pseudoclitocybe cyathiformis (Bull.) Singer (Polish: lejkownik kubkowatokapeluszowy) is a species of fungus in the family Pseudoclitocybaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap Diameter 4–10 cm, the shape goblet-shaped or deeply funnel-shaped with inrolled margins. It is hygrophanous and slightly shiny. In dry weather the skin is smooth and light coffee-coloured or flesh-coloured, in wet weather from dark umber through coffee-brown to chocolate-brown. Gills Thick, distant, fairly deeply decurrent on the stem, forked. Their colour ranges from whitish through light brown to red-brown. Stem Height 5–12 cm, thickness 0.5–1.2 cm, the shape cylindrical, club-like thickened at the base. The colour is brown, with a felty surface covered with fibrils or netted. Flesh Watery and soft, brownish in colour, with an indistinct smell and taste. Spore print White. Similar species: Pseudoclitocybe expallens (Polish: lejkownik bezwonny). It is smaller, and only very young specimens have an inrolled margin; Cantharellula umbonata (Polish: pieprzniczka szarawa). Its flesh and gills change colour to reddish when pressed; Infundibulicybe gibba (Polish: lejkogłówka żółtobrązowa) has a pale ochre cap.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe and Japan. In Poland it is common. Saprotroph. It occurs in various types of forests, but also in grass outside forests. It grows on a layer of humus on the ground, also on dead tree trunks and on wood remains mixed with soil. Fruiting bodies appear only in late autumn, rarely earlier than October. Sometimes they can develop even on damp stones.
Pseudohydnum gelatinosum (Scop.) P. Karst. (Polish: galaretek kolczasty) is a species of fungus in the order Auriculariales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Tremelloid, containing a great deal of water. After drying only a thin flake remains of it. It consists of a spatula-shaped (tongue-shaped, bracket-shaped) cap and an eccentrically set short stem. It may also be attached by its side to the wood (without a stem). The colour is whitish with a bluish tinge. The upper surface is granular or warty. The width of the fruiting body across the top is 1–8 cm. Besides white specimens there are specimens with a grey or pink-brown colouring of the upper side of the cap. Hymenophore: Spiny, the colour of the fruiting body. The spines are fairly dense, up to 3 mm long. Flesh: Whitish with a pale bluish tinge, jelly-like in consistency, watery, slightly translucent (glassy), without taste or smell. Spore print: Colourless to white. Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 3.5–6.5 × 5–8.5 μm. Similar species: Hyalodon piceicola (Polish: pierwoząb świerkowy). It has a flat, spread-out fruiting body and in Poland its occurrence has been reported only in the Białowieża Forest. It cannot be confused with other white and gelatinous fungi occurring in Poland, because it has a spiny hymenophore.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Apart from Antarctica and Africa it has been recorded on all continents, and also on many islands. In Poland it is common. A tree-dwelling saprotrophic fungus. It grows in mixed and coniferous forests. It occurs in groups of several specimens growing like roof tiles throughout the year. Most often in summer and autumn, usually on dead spruce and pine wood. In Poland it appears from summer to autumn, and sometimes it can also be met in spring and winter.
Pseudoinonotus dryadeus (Pers.) Murrill (Polish: bladoporek płaczący) is a species of fungus in the family Hymenochaetaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: An annual bracket fungus, growing singly, or in groups of several specimens like roof tiles. It has a hemispherical, bracket-shaped or shelf-shaped form and a width of 10–25 cm. The margin is blunt and mostly even. It attaches to the substrate by its side. The upper surface is velvety or rough, uneven, pitted or lumpy, at first cream, then orange-brown, ochre, rusty or tobacco-coloured. A characteristic feature is the presence on the surface of numerous drops of red-brown liquid. After drying, brown depressions remain in their place. The flesh is watery and spongy in young fruiting bodies, dry, fibrous and corky in older ones. It is tawny to rusty red and indistinctly zoned. The hymenophore is on the lower surface, tubular, at first whitish-grey, then yellow-brown. The tubes form one layer. They have round, white, frosted pores and are 5–20 mm long. There are 2–5 per 1 mm. In older fruiting bodies they are often overgrown with a whitish-yellowish layer of mycelium. The fruiting body has a fairly strong and unpleasant smell. The taste is mild, slightly sour. Microscopic features: Monomitic hyphal system.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs throughout the Northern Hemisphere, mainly in the temperate climate zone. It has also been recorded in Hawaii, South Africa and Australia. In Poland it is rare. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – species vulnerable to extinction. It is on lists of threatened species also in Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Lithuania and Sweden. It occurs in forests and parks on living trees. In Europe and Asia it occurs on oaks, but in Mexico and California mainly on firs. In California its occurrence has also been recorded on cedars and pines.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: More frequent is Inocutis dryophila (Polish: błyskoporek dębowy). It is distinguished by smaller, hoof-shaped fruiting bodies, which in the central part of the cap have a hard, darker, yellow-veined and granular insert.
Psilocybe semilanceata (Fr.) P. Kumm. (Polish: łysiczka lancetowata) is a species of fungus in the family Agrocybaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 1–2 cm, hygrophanous; when wet it is olive to light brown, also with dark olive or blue-green spots (especially on the circumference); dried, it takes on a colour from pale straw to ochre. The surface is smooth, moist, slimy, slightly sticky. The shape is at first bluntly conical and usually with a sharp papilla in the centre, with age conical to bell-shaped, but never spread out. Gills: Broad, narrowly adnate to the stem. Light brown in young fruiting bodies, darker in older ones – tobacco-brown. The edges are paler. The number of gills is 15–27. Stem: Thin, 3–15 cm tall and 1–3 mm in diameter. It is flexible, cylindrical and hollow inside, sometimes only widened at the base, mostly bent. The surface is pale ochre, smooth or longitudinally fibrillose. Flesh: Beige when dry, grey-brown when wet, without taste and without smell. Microscopic features: Spore print dark brown. Spores oblong, oval, measuring 10.5–15 × 6.5–8.5 μm. Basidia 4-spored, measuring 20–31 × 5–9 μm; they have clamp connections at the base. On the gill edges there are cheilocystidia measuring 15–30 × 4–7 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: The occurrence of this species has been described in North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and in Chile in South America. In Europe it occurs in Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, the Channel Islands, the Czech Republic, Denmark, Estonia, the Faroe Islands, Finland, France, Germany, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Russia, Slovakia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and England. In Poland it is not very frequent – mainly on mountain pastures and in the foothills.
Postia ptychogaster (F. Ludw.) Vesterh. (Polish: miękkoporek sproszkowany, drobnoporek sproszkowany) is a species of fungus in the family Dacryobolaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Fruiting body: Annual. It attaches to the substrate by its side. Fruiting bodies grow singly or in a few clusters. A single one has a diameter of up to 10 cm, and is cushion-shaped or semicircular. The surface is hairy, white in young fruiting bodies, turning brown in older ones. Hymenophore: Tubular, it forms in the lower part of the fruiting body, sparsely and late, and it disintegrates quickly, as a result of which it is fairly hard to observe. The tubes are brittle and short, their pores are torn, with 2–4 per mm. Flesh: Juicy in young fruiting bodies, harder only at the base. It consists of radially arranged fibrils separated by cavities filled with chlamydospores. It is concentrically zoned. Spores: The chlamydospores are ovoid-ellipsoid and thick-walled, measuring 4.7 × 3.4–4.5 μm. The basidiospores are ellipsoid, ending in an oblique beak, smooth, colourless and usually with a droplet. They measure 4–5.5 × 2.5–3.5 μm. Similar species: Postia stiptica (Polish: gorzkobiałak trzoneczkowy) does not have such a hairy surface and is bitter in taste; similar hairy fruiting bodies of the imperfect form also occur in other species of the genera Postia and Tyromyces, but rarely and they are smaller.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe, Russia and in the province of Quebec in Canada. In Poland it is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is R – potentially threatened because of its limited geographical range and small habitat areas, although according to other sources it is rather common. It grows in mixed forests, above all on coniferous trees, especially on pine and spruce; it has also been recorded on the larch Larix kaempferi. On deciduous trees it occurs less often. It is a saprotroph developing on dead wood and causing brown rot of wood.
Pycnoporellus fulgens (Fr.) Donk (Polish: pomarańczowiec błyszczący) is a species of fungus in the order Polyporales.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Habit: A bracket fungus with an annual fruiting body, which attaches to the substrate by its side, and is sometimes spread out and reflexed. Fruiting body: Fruiting bodies occur singly or in groups of several, often arranged like roof tiles one above another. A single fruiting body is semicircular, fan-shaped or bracket-shaped, up to 10 cm wide and up to 3 cm thick. Its base is often narrowed. The surface is uneven, wrinkled and radially furrowed. Young specimens are felty and rough, older ones bare and usually matt. The colour is orange or brick-red. Flesh: Spongy and juicy in young specimens, fibrous in older ones. After drying it becomes light, corky and brittle, and also changes colour to apricot-orange. Under the action of KOH it darkens and becomes raspberry-coloured. Hymenophore: Tubular, consisting of one layer of tubes 3–5 mm long. The inner walls of the tubes are often covered with a white bloom. The pores of the tubes are angular, of irregular or maze-like shape. They are 0.4 to 1 mm in diameter. In young specimens the pores are orange-brick, in older ones tawny, brittle, torn and toothed. The taste is sourish, astringent, the smell unpleasant. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in the Northern Hemisphere. In Poland it is rare. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is V – a vulnerable species which in the near future will move into the category of species vulnerable to extinction if the threatening factors do not cease to operate. It is on lists of threatened species also in Germany, Denmark, Norway and Finland. In Poland it is found in coniferous or mixed forests. It develops on dead wood, especially of firs and spruces. Its occurrence on deciduous trees, in particular on birches and poplars, has been observed only sporadically.
Rhodocollybia butyracea (Bull.) Lennox (Polish: monetnica maślana) is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–7 cm, arched in young individuals, spread out with an umbo in the middle in older ones. It is very water-absorbent. In wet weather, after soaking up water, it is coloured from grey through rusty brown to red-brown, in dry periods from pale ochre to grey-white. The cap margin and the umbo are usually darker. The skin is smooth. Gills: The gills are white, attached only shortly at the top and therefore looking almost free. Stem: Light brown to red-brown, covered with white, fibrous fibrils. The base often looks swollen, hollow, longitudinally grooved on the outside. A very characteristic feature is the cartilaginous nature of the stem: the outer layer is elastic and rubbery, the inner one has cottony-foamy flesh. Flesh: The flesh is thin, watery, soft. In the cap it is elastic, inside the stem cartilaginous. In wet weather it is brownish, in dry weather whitish. The taste and smell are indistinct, resembling the smell of rancid butter. Spore print: White. Spores ellipsoid, smooth, measuring 6–7.5 × 3–3.5 µm in diameter. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is most numerous in Europe and North America; beyond these continents its localities have also been listed in Argentina and Japan. In Europe it is very common. It grows from summer to late autumn in both deciduous and coniferous forests, mostly on acid soils. In Poland it is also common.
Rhodocollybia maculata (Alb. & Schwein.) Singer (Polish: monetnica plamista) is a species of fungus in the family Omphalotaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–10 cm, hemispherical in young individuals, arched in older ones, finally spread out with a blunt umbo. The cap margin stays inrolled for a long time. It is not water-absorbent. The skin of the cap is smooth, coloured from white to yellowish-cream. A characteristic feature is the occurrence of rusty spots on the skin, and with age there are more and more of them, so that in older specimens the whole skin becomes uniformly rusty brown. Gills: Narrow, crowded and running down the stem with a tooth. They are white, but change colour to red-brown when pressed. The gill edges are weakly toothed, in older specimens covered with rusty spots. Stem: Height 6–10 cm, diameter 1–2 cm, cylindrical, hard and often bent. Sometimes it widens at the base, while below it it is pointed. It is solid, and only in old specimens does it become hollow inside. It has a colour similar to the cap and with time is also spotted rusty, and in older specimens rusty. Flesh: Springy, whitish, gradually darkening when damaged. It smells of sawdust, the taste is bitter. Spore print: Pale cream. Spores smooth, elliptical-round, measuring 4–5 × 5–6 μm. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It is known mainly in North America and Europe, but its occurrence has also been recorded in Central Africa and in Costa Rica (Central America). In Central Europe it is common. In Poland it is also common. It occurs mainly on litter in coniferous forests, although it is also found in mixed forests. It grows mainly under spruces and pines, usually in groups.
Rhodotus palmatus (Bull.) Maire (Polish: żyłkowiec różowawy) is a species of fungus in the family Physalacriaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Of a bright pink-salmon colour; the gelatinous skin of young fruiting bodies is covered with a very distinct network of white veins; diameter 1.5–9 cm. Gills: Adnate to notched, crowded, up to 11 mm wide, unforked, pale reddish, non-staining; edges even, gills in 2 to 4 tiers. Stem: Short, measuring 1.5–3 × 0.4–1 cm, usually eccentric. The surface is dry, covered with a very thin layer of short, vertical, delicate, white hairs that rub off easily. Flesh: Solid, pale pink to cream, non-staining, up to 8 mm thick. The taste is bitter. The smell is not characteristic, slightly fruity, somewhat sharply aromatic. Microscopic features: Spore print pinkish. Basidia club-shaped, 4-spored, measuring 33.6–43.2 × 5.6–8 μm. The contents are finely granular with numerous large oily droplets; hyaline in KOH. Basidiospores spherical to ovoid, warted with thin walls, measuring 6–8.7 × 6–7.4 µm, hyaline in KOH and non-amyloid. Pleurocystidia absent. Cheilocystidia numerous, measuring 27.2–48 × 13–25 μm, spindle-shaped to bottle-shaped with exceptionally long and narrow bases, walls smooth, thin.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in many European countries (including Scandinavia), North Africa, the eastern part of North America and Canada, Korea and Japan. A species with a circumboreal range. In Poland it is rare; after more than a hundred years it was recorded in Poland at only one locality in the Białowieża Forest, although according to a 2010 study it is clearly spreading there. In 2020 it was already known from 6 localities. In Poland it is under strict protection. Threat category E (Endangered).
Rickenella fibula (Bull.) Raithelh. (Polish: spinka pomarańczowa) is a species of fungus in the family Rickenellaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–15 mm, at first bell-shaped-arched, then arched, finally with a depressed centre. The margin is wavy, grooved and toothed. The surface is sticky, coloured from orange-yellow to orange, faded in older specimens, even to whitish. Gills: Distant and running down the stem, with short intermediate gills, at first whitish, then yellowish, finally light orange. Stem: Height 2–5 cm, thickness 1–1 mm, thin, cylindrical. Under a magnifying glass the surface is finely speckled, yellowish in young specimens, orange-brown in older ones. Spore print: White. Microscopic features: Spores 3–4 × 1.5–2.5 µm, ellipsoid, smooth, hyaline with 1 to 3 guttules, non-amyloid in KOH. Cheilocystidia and pleurocystidia 25–40 × 5–7.5 µm, spindle-shaped with tapering or rounded tips, thin-walled, hyaline in KOH, smooth. In the skin there are tightly packed hyphae with numerous pileocystidia 50–100 × 7.5–12.5 µm, spindle-shaped with broad bases and conical or head-like tips, thin-walled, smooth, hyaline in KOH. Similar species:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: Rickenella fibula occurs on all continents; a locality has even been reported in Antarctica. In Europe it is widespread, from the Mediterranean to Spitsbergen. In Poland it is very common. A ground-dwelling saprotrophic fungus. It occurs in forests, especially pine forests, among grasses and brushwood, in wetlands, heaths and wet meadows, usually in damp places among mosses. It is associated with mosses, probably parasitises them, or forms some kind of mycorrhiza with them. In Poland it forms fruiting bodies from May to October.
Rubroboletus satanas (Lenz) Kuan Zhao & Zhu L. Yang (Polish: krwistoborowik szatański, borowik szatański) is a species of fungus in the family Boletaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 6–30 cm, grey, in mature individuals with a yellowish or greenish tinge, brown-ochre when pressed. Hemispherical, later bent and flattened, thick. The skin is matt, dry or suede-like, and does not separate from the flesh. Tubes: At first yellowish, then blood-red, with age taking on a brown-olive colour. When damaged they turn blue. The pores in young ones are at first orange-yellow, later carmine, and in old specimens become olive. Stem: Height 5–15 cm, thickness 3–8 cm. Solid, massive, at first spherical or cylindrical, then barrel-shaped. Under the cap it is yellowish, lower down it is carmine-red. Flesh: Whitish, fleshy, slowly turning blue after cutting. The taste is mild, the smell weak; old individuals have a smell somewhat resembling carrion. Spore print: Olive. Spores smooth, ellipsoid, measuring 10 × 16 × 5–7 μm. Similar species: Rubroboletus rhodoxanthus (Polish: krwistoborowik purpurowy). It is also rare, has a red stem and its flesh turns blue (but only on the cap). It differs in the pink tinge of the cap, the stem is cylindrical, covered with a characteristic network. Caloboletus calopus (Polish: gorzkoborowik żółtopory).

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs only in Europe. It is rare everywhere. In Poland it is very rare, dying out. It is on the Red List of plants and fungi of Poland. Its status is E – endangered, critically threatened. It is on lists of threatened species also in Austria, Belgium, the Czech Republic, Germany, Denmark, Slovakia, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden, Estonia and England. One of its localities was found in an orchid beech wood in the Kaczawskie Mountains, and another was discovered in 2006 in a warm beech wood on the Kraków-Częstochowa Upland.
Russula aeruginea Lindblad ex Fr. (Polish: gołąbek białozielonawy, gołąbek grynszpanowy) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 3–10 cm. Young fruiting bodies have a spherical cap, in older ones it becomes broadly spread out and depressed in the middle. The surface is smooth, dry and matt, crenate at the margin. In rain it becomes slimy. The colour is from green through olive-green to yellow-green. In the middle it is mostly darker. The skin can be peeled off almost from the whole cap. Gills: Broad, crowded and of varying length. Not attached to the stem, or only slightly. White in young individuals, cream in older ones. Stem: Smooth and cylindrical, white, rusty-spotted at the base, pointed, without a ring. Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm. Solid in young specimens, spongy inside in older ones. Flesh: Hard, white and brittle in young specimens. It has a slightly burning taste, especially the gills. Under the action of FeSO4 it becomes greyish-pink. Spore print: Pale cream. Spores ellipsoid or obovoid, covered with small warts. The warts are up to 0.6 μm high, with blunt tips, some of them joined by single, delicate connections. Dimensions: 7–10 × 6–7 μm. Cystidia blunt or with a broad tip at the top, dermatocystidia cylindrical, blunt.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America and Europe. In Poland it is one of the most frequently occurring brittlegills. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows in deciduous, coniferous and mixed forests, also in parks, on litter, mainly under silver birch and downy birch, less often under sycamore maple, beech, spruce, pine and black locust. Fruiting bodies grow from June to November.
Russula atropurpurea (Krombh.) Britzelm. (Polish: gołąbek ciemnopurpurowy) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, later flat-arched with a depression in the middle. The margins are often wavy, sometimes lobed. The skin is smooth; in dry weather it is shiny, in wet weather slimy. It can be peeled off to half the diameter of the cap. The cap margin is not moderately blunt, wavy and uniform, only in older specimens sometimes slightly crenate. The cap skin is characterised by vivid colours and a great variety of colouring forms. In typical cases the cap is dark red, blood-red, crimson, purple-red, or even red-black. There are, however, forms with a strongly pink, red-violet, dirty lilac or grey-olive-brown cap. Gills: Narrow, crowded and brittle. They are coloured from white to pale cream, and in older mushrooms become rusty-spotted. Stem: Height 4–6 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, cylindrical. At first hard and compact, with time it becomes spongy. It is white and slightly greyish, only at the base weakly rusty. Flesh: White, hard, only directly under the skin reddish-violet. The taste is stinging, especially in young mushrooms. Spore print: White. Microscopic features:

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in Europe and South America. Its occurrence has also been described in Morocco, Korea and Japan. In Poland it is frequent. In Polish mycological literature it has been described at numerous localities throughout the country. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in deciduous and mixed forests in which pine or oak occurs.
Russula claroflava Grove (Polish: gołąbek jasnożółty) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–10 cm, hemispherical in youth with an inrolled margin, then flat, with a depression in the middle, hard and fleshy. The surface is glossy, uniformly coloured, lemon-yellow to chrome-yellow. The skin can be removed to half the cap. Gills: Thick and fairly distant, sometimes forked or forming anastomoses. Rounded at the margin, narrowed at the stem, free, or slightly decurrent with a tooth. At first white, later yellow-ochre. Stem: Height 4–7 cm, thickness 1.5–2.5 cm, cylindrical, sometimes slightly widened in the middle, first solid, then cottony. The surface is white, sometimes slightly lemon-tinged, almost smooth or suede-like. It turns grey when touched. Flesh: Thick and firm, white. When cut it changes colour to blackish-grey. The taste is at first astringent, later mild and sweetish. The smell is weak. Spore print: Ochre. Microscopic features: Numerous laticifers occur in the cortex of the stem. Spores broadly ellipsoid, measuring 8.5–12 × 6–9 μm. The surface is warty-reticulate, the warts conical, medium-sized, the reticulum very delicate. Basidia measuring 35–50 × 10–12 μm.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in North America, Europe and Japan. In Polish mycological literature it has been described at numerous localities. It is probably not rare. A ground-dwelling mycorrhizal fungus. It grows in damp and dark deciduous forests with scattered birches or in boggy birch woods, sometimes also on peat bogs. It produces fruiting bodies from July to October.
Russula cyanoxantha (Schaeff.) Fr. (Polish: gołąbek zielonawofioletowy) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–15 cm. Hemispherical when young with a bent margin, later convex, when old concave to funnel-shaped. The skin is mostly without gloss. In wet weather the skin is sticky, in dry weather shiny. There is great variability in the colouring of the cap. It is coloured in various shades of violet, blue, pink, ochre, olive and grey-blackish. The whole cap may be uniformly coloured, but may also be a combination of the colours listed. Gills: The gills are white, fairly crowded, of varying length (short gills mixed with longer ones). They are flexible (they do not crumble when touched with a finger) – which is an exception among brittlegills. This species is the only brittlegill whose gills do not become brittle in older mushrooms but retain their elasticity. Stem: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 2–3 cm, cylindrical, at first hard, later spongy. White, rarely tinged lilac-red. Flesh: Permanently white, fairly compact. The taste is mild. Unlike other brittlegills, the flesh does not turn pinkish-flesh-coloured under the action of ferrous sulphate. Microscopic features: Spore print white.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs in Europe, North and Central America, Asia and Australia. In Poland it is very common. A ground-dwelling fungus. It grows from July to October, mostly in deciduous forests, less often coniferous ones, mainly under oaks or beeches. It grows on various soils, avoiding only calcareous soils. In Central Europe and in Poland it is fairly frequent.
Russula decolorans Fr. (Polish: gołąbek płowiejący) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 5–12 cm. At first almost spherical, later flattened, usually orange or brick-red. Older caps fade and become ochre and sometimes have slightly striate cap margins. The cap surface is smooth, sticky in wet weather, dry in dry weather. Gills: Free, crowded, broad, ventricose and somewhat fragile. At first white, later butter-yellow. Older ones blacken on the surface, and turn grey when damaged. Stem: Cylindrical, 2 to 8 cm long and 1 to 3 cm thick, white. Old stems become dark grey or blackish. They turn grey when damaged. Flesh: Whitish, sometimes slightly yellowish under the cap skin. When cut or with age it turns grey or blackens. It has no smell, the taste is mild. Spore print: Pale ochre. Microscopic features: Spores varied in size, mostly measuring 10–13 × 10–12 μm, broadly ellipsoid or obovoid, strongly warty; the warts are large, from conical and blunt to sharp, in places joined by connections. The suprahilar spot is amyloid in Melzer's reagent.

sections.head: Distribution
sections.text: It occurs in North and Central America, in Europe, Asia and Africa. In Poland it is common. A ground-dwelling fungus. It occurs fairly commonly on boggy and acid soils, in coniferous forests especially on sandy soils. Fruiting bodies appear from July to October.
Russula nigricans Fr. (Polish: gołąbek czarniawy) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 10–20 cm, arched in youth, then spread out and depressed in the middle. It has inrolled margins, and is very hard and thick-fleshed. Young specimens are whitish, then whitish-olive-grey, later dark brown, finally black. Gills: Distant. Very thick, brittle, lobed and slightly attached to the stem. Like the cap they are white in youth, then gradually change colour to black. When damaged they turn grey, and even black. Stem: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 1–3 cm. It is thick, cylindrical, solid and very hard. Compared with most brittlegill species it is short. Like the cap it changes colour during development from white to black. When pressed it reddens. Flesh: It is very hard; when cut it first reddens, then blackens; the smell is very weak and somewhat insipid, the taste mild. Microscopic features: Spore print white. Spores of a shape from spherical to obovoid-broad, measuring 6–8 × 6–7 μm. The surface is covered with small warts and a faintly outlined reticulum. Basidia measuring 40–60 × 6–10 μm. Cystidia numerous, measuring 70–80 × 5–7 μm, narrow and projecting 20–30 μm above the hymenium.

sections.head: Distribution and habitat
sections.text: It occurs mainly in North and Central America and Europe, and also in Morocco in Africa, in Korea, Japan and Australia. In Poland it is fairly common. It grows in deciduous and coniferous forests, under beeches and firs. Fruiting bodies appear from July to November.

sections.head: Similar species
sections.text: There are many brittlegill species that blacken immediately when damaged. Similar may be Russula densifolia (Polish: gołąbek gęstoblaszkowy), but it has more crowded gills; Russula albonigra (Polish: gołąbek białoczarny) with a bitterish-minty taste; or Russula adusta (Polish: gołąbek podpalany), but its cap is paler at the margins, and its flesh reddens after cutting but does not blacken.
Russula ochroleuca Fr. (Polish: gołąbek brudnożółty) is a species of fungus in the family Russulaceae.

sections.head: Morphology
sections.text: Cap: Diameter 4–8(10) cm, hemispherical in youth, later flat, wavy and slightly bent. The skin can be peeled off to about half the diameter of the cap. In wet weather it is sticky, in dry weather dry. The colour is yellowish-ochre to lemon. The cap skin is smooth. The margin is blunt and slightly bent, in older fruiting bodies sometimes slightly crenate and lumpy. Gills: Brittle, moderately crowded in young fruiting bodies, sparser later. They are free, and notched in a sinus shape at the stem, rounded at the margin, sometimes forked. At first white, with time pale cream, and ochre spots appear on them in places.
